paper.title: The education-health gradient: Revisiting the role of socio-emotional skills
paper.code_data_availability: No data- or code-availability statement is printed in the article. …

registers.name_in_paper: a tailor-made online survey in Denmark (BFI-2 personality inventory, Locus of Control, economic preferences, self-reported health and health behaviors)
variables_mentioned: BFI-2 (60- or 30-item) Big Five traits and 15 facets
internal Locus of Control index (7 items)
self-rated Health Status (1 = excellent to 5 = bad)

registers.name_in_paper: the administrative registers / Danish administrative registers
variables_mentioned: family income quartiles within 5-year age groups

registers.role: linkage / sample frame (siblings are persons with the same biological or adoptive mother)

registers.name_in_paper: hospital register data / hospital records (detailed health diagnoses and health-care use)
variables_mentioned: hospital diagnoses (ICD-10) for the Charlson Comorbidity Index

linkages: The completed survey data was anonymized and merged to the administrative registers by Statistics Denmark, via the common unique personal identifier for all individuals in Denmark
Siblings are persons with the same mother (biological or adoptive) in the population registers from 1986-2019

sample.universe: A random sample of 121,390 individuals in Denmark in 2019, drawn by Statistics Denmark and representative of each cohort from 1944-2001; for the cohorts born 1956-1998 the siblings of non-singleton individuals were also identified
sample.unit_of_observation: individual survey respondent linked to the administrative registers
selection_rules: All individuals 18 and older were contacted in May and August 2019 via the secure messaging system e-Boks; the response rate was 33.7% including partial responses and 30% for complete responses
Out of 41,373 respondents to the survey, 38,799 had complete BFI facet scales
Adding the availability of Locus of Control results in 37,847 respondents
The age restriction (aged 25-75 in 2019, to ensure educational attainment is completed) limits the sample to 31,391; these also have full education information
Of these, 28,692 responded to the questions on patience and risk
A further restriction to non-missing personal and family income gives the full survey sample of 28,261

Sibling sample: 69,749 individuals received an invitation together with at least one sibling; 12,228 siblings responded in pairs (or more) from the same family; adding the main-sample restrictions results in 9,023 individuals from 4,062 families (73% of responses from sibling pairs, 22% from 3 responses per family)
sample.period: Survey fielded May and August 2019; health outcomes measured in 2018 (CCI from diagnoses 1999-2018); income measured in 2014
sample.n_observations: 28,261 (full survey sample); 9,023 (sibling sample); column-specific N in Table 3 ranges from 8,598 to 9,023
sample.n_individuals: 28,261 individuals in the full survey sample; 9,023 individuals from 4,062 families in the sibling sample

construction_notes: All Big Five traits, facets and Locus of Control are residuals from a regression of each trait or facet on five-year age bins among all respondents, standardized to mean zero and standard deviation one in the sample
BMI is computed from the survey answers on weight and height
Self-reported Health Status is on a scale 1-5, where a higher score indicates worse health; the MHI-5 ranges from 5-30 with a higher score indicating greater distress
The Charlson Comorbidity Index uses the updated weights of Quan et al. (2011) and the ICD-10 conversion of Quan et al. (2005), collapsing any diagnosis of illnesses in the past 20 years (1999-2018)
Nights hospitalized is the count of total nights hospitalized in 2018, excluding hospitalizations or visits for preventive care, screening, or pregnancy- or birth-related reasons
Personal disposable income is measured in 2014, four years before the health outcomes: labour income plus transfers net of income taxes, in 10,000 Danish Kroner
Family income quartiles are formed within each 5-year age group from personal disposable income among all household members, averaged with the OECD equivalency scales

The Big Five traits and the 15 facets cannot be included simultaneously because the traits are functions of the facets and collinear; the Big Five contribution is obtained from a separate 'full' model containing the Big Five traits only instead of the facets, with the same set of other covariates
Contributions of covariate groups to the gradient are estimated with the order-invariant decomposition of Gelbach (2016), built on the baseline Eq. (1) and the full Eq. (2)

claims.statement: Within sibling pairs, an additional year of completed education is associated with lower BMI (Body Mass Index) (the education-health gradient that remains after the contribution of sibling fixed effects is netted out).

register_source.value: Danish administrative registers (years of education); no register code named in the paper

definition.value: Years of completed education recorded in the Danish administrative registers; the sample is restricted to ages 25-75 in 2019 to ensure that educational attainment is completed

timing.value: Completed educational attainment as of the register year, measured before the 2018/2019 health outcomes

definition.value: Body-mass Index, computed from the survey answers on weight and height

timing.value: Self-reported in the 2019 survey, concurrent with the measurement of personality

units.value: BMI points per additional year of education

magnitude.interpretation: A single year of education reduces BMI by .123, implying that a university degree versus high school (five extra years) would reduce BMI by .615. This corresponds to 12% of a standard deviation (see Table 2).

population.period: Survey fielded May and August 2019; hospital outcomes measured in 2018 (CCI diagnoses 1999-2018); income measured in 2014

identification.source_of_variation: Within-family differences in completed years of education between siblings (persons with the same mother in the population registers 1986-2019) in a survey that over-sampled siblings

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on family (sibling) indicators and the included covariates, the remaining within-family variation in education is unrelated to unobserved determinants of health -- the sibling-fixed-effects design absorbs shared genetic endowments and childhood environment
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued in Section 2.4.1; the thought experiment of comparing two siblings with the same early childhood conditions, partially shared genes and observable characteristics but different educational attainment; precedents cited (Amin et al., 2015; Halpern-Manners et al., 2020; Lleras-Muney et al., 2022; Fletcher and Lehrer, 2011; Fletcher, 2013)

rhs: unobserved determinants of BMI (Body Mass Index)

key_assumptions.assumption: Causality runs from socio-emotional skills to health and education, not from health back to personality (no reverse causality)
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 2.4.3 reviews panel and natural-experiment evidence that personality traits in adults do not change systematically in response to health shocks or life events (Cobb-Clark and Schurer, 2012, 2013; Specht et al., 2011; Damian et al., 2021; Bleidorn et al., 2021)

implies_edges.to: socio-emotional skills (Big Five traits/facets, Locus of Control)

key_assumptions.assumption: Education does not itself produce socio-emotional skills, so skills are an omitted variable rather than a mediator of education
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 2.4.3 and the conclusion: the authors concede they cannot exclude mediation but judge the evidence for general education driving socio-emotional skills to be weak (Kassenboehmer et al., 2018; Dahmann and Anger, 2018; Dobbie and Fryer, 2015; West et al., 2015)

implies_edges.to: socio-emotional skills (Big Five traits/facets, Locus of Control)

key_assumptions.assumption: Any unobserved endowment that differs between siblings within a family remains an unresolved common cause of education and health -- the authors concede family fixed effects cannot absorb it
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 2.4.1: 'unobserved family factors may not be entirely common within siblings/twins'; references to parental reinforcement/compensation (Behrman et al., 1982; Price, 2008) and to polygenic-score studies (Amin et al., 2023; Lleras-Muney et al., 2022)

implies_edges.from: within-sibling differences in genetic factors and early endowments (unobserved)
within-sibling differences in genetic factors and early endowments (unobserved)

key_assumptions.assumption: Selection into the estimation sample -- survey response (33.7%) and both siblings of a family responding -- does not distort the estimated gradient
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 2.3 and footnote 7: sibling respondents are positively selected on demographics and if anything negatively selected on health, but the distributions overlap heavily (Fig. S.2) and Inverse Probability Weighting yields remarkably similar results

threats_discussed: Sibling fixed effects do not necessarily lead to causal estimates of the education-health gradient (Galama et al., 2018)
Unobserved family factors may not be entirely common within siblings/twins: wombmates may compete for resources, and parents may reinforce or compensate differences in innate endowments
Remaining within-sibling differences in education may not be exogenous despite the list of covariates
Reverse causality from health to self-reported personality traits
Education itself may shape socio-emotional skills, making personality a mediator rather than an omitted variable
Lack of research on the effects of health shocks on personality facets (as opposed to traits)
Selection into survey response (33.7% response rate) and positive selection of sibling respondents on demographics
Non-classical measurement error in BMI
robustness_checks: Gelbach (2016) order-invariant decomposition instead of sequentially adding covariates and attributing the reduction to the latest added covariate
Same decomposition repeated in the full sample of survey respondents ignoring family effects (Appendix Tables S.19 to S.21), with remarkably similar patterns of relative importance
Inverse Probability Weighting for the propensity to respond, based on the covariates in Table 2, yields remarkably similar results (footnote 7)
Heterogeneity analyses by age and gender (Appendix Fig. S.8 and Tables S.22 to S.25)
unresolved_confounders: Within-sibling variation in genetic factors or early endowments that family fixed effects cannot absorb
Possible mediation of education through socio-emotional skills ('we cannot exclude the mediation of education via increased socio-emotional skills')

Possible remaining endogeneity of within-sibling differences in education

estimator.value: OLS with family (sibling group) fixed effects; the reported figure is b_base from Eq. (1) net of the reduction attributed to the family indicators by the Gelbach (2016) decomposition

estimation.specification: Eq. (1) Y_ij = Edu_ij b_base + X^1_ij beta_1 + eps_ij, with the contribution of the family indicators Z_j of Eq. (2) netted out via the Gelbach (2016) order-invariant decomposition

mediators_claimed: Socio-emotional skills as a possible mediator of education ('we acknowledge that skills might partially mediate effects of education on health, but favor the interpretation of skills being an omitted variable')

heterogeneity.finding: The contribution of personality to the education-gradient in health does not vary consistently across gender- and age-groups; baseline education-health gradients are generally stronger for younger than for older people, especially for smoking (relegated to Appendix Fig. S.8 and Tables S.22 to S.25).
